content.text: High-school AP Literature hybrid essay responding to Lillian Boxfish Takes a Walk — personal reflection woven with close reading on hope, cynicism, and endurance.

Ever since a certain day at age eleven, I have contemplated the question- is the human race inherently good or bad? It was a debate tournament amongst college students that later came to define my ideology, though at that moment it had simply piqued my interest to know that the winning side argued that it was bad, a resolution quite unlike what I had imagined. When I asked my dad for his position, his answer was somewhere along the lines of inherent evilness, and then laughed a little at the cynicism of his response. He paused for a moment, thinking a little, and gave me a peculiar answer- humans are hopeful, but the reality is disappointing. While I cannot remember his exact words now, the implications lived with me through the years, and as I grew up, I learned the struggle of having both hopefulness and realism, or in my words- cynical idealism, a hopefulness dulled by the real world, but a cynicism too optimistic about the future.

I toy with the thought often, the juxtaposition of hope and hopelessness, and upon walking with Lillian Boxfish through her journey on New Year's Eve, I was reminded of the oxymoronic concept of a cynical idealist. As a cynical idealist herself, Lillian Boxfish portrays a conflicted ideology morphed through the reality of sexism and city violence but also the hopes of interpersonal connection and love. Kathleen Rooney argues for a need for hope and gratitude in an often disappointing reality through utilizing characterization and her metaphoric approach of painting Lillian’s life as a circle, ending Boxfish’s conflict with herself with the same metaphor as the beginning.

Throughout the book, Rooney paints Boxfish as a character that often appears undecided to readers as to the way that she approaches her life. While certain in her resolve to never marry, she falls in love faithfully, and while certain in her hate of certain things, seems to love others quite similar to those that she hates. However, the reason behind her characterization does not appear until the readers dive further into the book. Her struggles with her career, mental health, and sexism bring out the full Boxfish as a hopeful realist relentlessly continuing in her journey despite the struggles that she faces. Upon her journey on New Year's Eve, Boxfish revisits Delmonico’s to find a friendly family willing to ask her to sit with them. In their conversation, she describes, “the constant low-grade lunacy of life in the city--but I am surprised to find, and I think they are too, that our stories emphasize the serendipitous, even the magical. Our tone is that of conspirators, as though we are afraid to be overheard speaking fondly of a city that conventional wisdom declares beyond hope”(153). Here, Rooney uses the juxtaposition of diction choices to magnify both the “lunacy” and the “serendipitous” that is her life in the city. While their conversation begins with the negative, it gradually changes into a hopeful tone for a better future, a drastic change in connotation Boxfish herself seems to be equally surprised about. While she compares their conversation to conspiracies, a gesture at the commonly accepted realism, Rooney paints an upbeat mood to reflect the value of hopefulness in that commonly accepted pessimism. Here, the contrast between cynicism about the reality of the unsalvageable city versus the hopeful nature of her conspiracies brings out Rooney's argument for the value of hopefulness during despair. Upon leaving Delmonico’s, Boxfish finds herself almost in tears from her connection with the family, and how much their kindness softened her scars of the past and quelled her loneliness. With such an implication, Rooney argues for the value of finding happiness and having hope and gratitude during the downs of life.

In the last few pages of the book, we can further sense such a dynamic development of Boxfish’s mentality from her resolution with time and herself, admitting that “The future and I are just about even, our quarrel all but resolved. I welcome its coming, and I resolve to be attentive to the details of its arrival...waving as it comes into view, born toward the present on its road of anthracite” (284). Using personification to present her conflict with herself as her conflict with time, Boxfish looks back upon her life as a journey meant to be something greater than herself, an almost noble battle with an enemy she has learned to forgive. She reflects on all the negative things that she has ever experienced in her life and sums it up as one entire battle, which she is now past, and in turn, looks to the future with a new hopefulness despite her past struggles. Boxfish then hints at the end of her life in the future that is to come, bringing back the poetic symbol of the road of anthracite, a symbol presented in the very beginning of the book and representative of Boxfish’s life. Throughout her life, Boxfish has doubted her decisions, conscious of her differences, her critiques, and her fall from being the highest-paid advertising woman in the world, but in the end, when she finally expresses closure with herself, she finds that what she needed was her earliest, unwavering dream all along, and hopefulness for a future, no matter how short. By utilizing this form of structural callback, Rooney communicates the value of being gratuitous and hopeful through the worst of it all, because in the end, we would still come full circle in our journey in life, and that no matter what you do in life, it will all have been worth the struggle. Rooney glorifies the resolution, and the ups despite the downs, bringing Boxfish’s life full circle with a positive ending. With this artistic touch, she presents Boxfish’s entire life as an argument for remaining hopeful and gratuitous, making an example out of Boxfish’s seemingly downward spiral of life, but her remaining hope for her future. She makes a lesson out of the cynical idealism of Boxfish, and in turn inspires the readers to be hopeful during the lows of their lives.

Closing the book upon finishing the pages, I was hit face first with the implications that the adored cynical idealist represented in my life, and the debate that first introduced me to the concept of cynical idealism. While the concept had always existed, I had struggled to develop it further before I had encountered the complex characterization of Lillian Boxfish. I had always known myself to be cynically ideal, to marvel at kindness and sigh in disappointment at the world, and to dig myself out of emotional holes that I keep getting myself into. I recalled specifically the spring of my junior year when I was drowning in the stress that I put on myself while studying for my four AP tests. For almost two months I lacked sound sleep or a motivation to be joyous in school, repercussions of a mental burden too imminent to think clearly. I begged for the school year to end every day, and cried myself to sleep every other day. On the nights before each of my AP tests, I failed to sleep until four in the morning, when the birds had already begun to chirp and laugh at my lack of mental strength. Yet I had won my battle, though I could’ve easily canceled my AP tests as I had wished to do every day of those two dreadful months. Boxfish’s story gave me insight into how I managed to do it, and hints as to how I might avoid such a struggle again, which is to retain hope for a future, no matter how distant or near. While I don’t tell my friends this, I spent every single day of those two months praying, though I was all but religious before that. I meditated and sought intellectual clearance. I had my eyes on very foreseeable freedom, right when I finished my AP tests, and I looked forward to it daily. I still struggle with balancing my education and my mental health in my senior year. However, a hope for a brighter future in college and in life carries me forward, and I hope that they shall continue to be my motivation as I move forward in life. My past burdens of balancing stressors are behind me, though I still have a whole life ahead full of as much joy as stress. Knowing now that my struggles are, as Rooney implies, but a small part of the battle, I have already learned to let go of some of my burdens, seeing as I no longer spend all my free time locking myself up and studying my weekends away, trapping myself in the lows of my emotional health. I cannot say I was very bright and hopeful then or now, but my lingering hopes as a cynical idealist propels me forward, and it gives me the motivation to make the world better. As a cynical idealist, I often feel the swinging mood of a pendulum, but then I remember that humans are inherently bad to begin with, as per the ending decision from the famous debate. However, the fact that there is happiness and kindness in the world means that people are trying to make the world a brighter place, that they are purposefully being bright and welcoming, hopeful and gratuitous. While I will leave high school for a university soon, I strive to bring as much passion into my life as I can, although I have a right to be pessimistic sometimes, because that is the reality of a cynical idealist.
